item.title: The Hidden Lifespan Risk in Men
item.description:
Loneliness

The Hidden Lifespan Risk in Men

Why men are dying younger, and it's not the reason you think.

Posted August 2, 2026

Key points
  • The male life expectancy gap isn't biology since it swings from 2.5 to 12.7 years by country.
  • Road traffic, drugs, and suicide drive most excess male deaths.
  • Harvard's 85-year study: Relationship satisfaction predicted longevity better than genetics.
  • Married men gain seven to 17 years of life which is more than women gain from marriage.
Being lonely hurts more than you think.
Source: Photo by Allen Shen / Pexels

My dad did not have many friends. I could count them on one hand. He was not a social man in the traditional sense. But he moved. He went places. The hardware store. The mall. His favorite, by far, was the airport. He would sit and watch planes take off, watch people say hello and goodbye to each other. That was his version of being around people.

Then COVID shut it all down.

No more hardware stores. No more malls. No more airports. Just the house, and the TV, and my mother.

Something in him changed. He got angrier. He watched more television than I had ever seen him watch. Not long after, he had a stroke. The stroke led to dementia, then he was diagnosed with Alzheimer's. The slide from there was fast. He died before my mother (who is still alive), just short of 85.

His father lived to 90. His grandfather made it to 95, and his grandfather's wife to 99. But it was not just that he died younger than the men before him. It was how those last years went.

I keep coming back to the math. Two generations of men in his own family made it well past 90. He did not, and the way he did not haunts me more than the number itself. I keep asking the same question: How much of that gap, in years and in quality, was COVID, and the isolation it forced on a man whose entire social life was built on simply being out in the world?

The Male-Female Life Expectancy Gap

I used to think men just die younger than women. It felt like gravity. A fact of life nobody questions.

A recent policy analysis from the American Institute for Boys and Men looked at the male-female life expectancy gap across wealthy countries and found something men rarely hear about themselves: the size of the gap swings wildly, from as little as 2.5 years to as much as 12.7 years, depending on the country. In most places, it has been shrinking for decades.

If this were pure biology, the gap would look the same everywhere. It doesn't. Lithuania cut its own gap by tightening road safety laws. Nothing about male chromosomes changed. The roads got safer, and fewer men died on them. That's the part that I found interesting. If a change in traffic enforcement can add years back to men's lives, then "men just die younger" is not a fact of life. It's a description of conditions we have decided to accept.

article continues after advertisement

What's Actually Killing Men Early

The above analysis points to three causes doing most of the damage to men's life expectancy: road traffic deaths, drug use disorders, and suicide. Road traffic is not a loneliness story. Men drive more miles, take more risks behind the wheel, and die in crashes at higher rates than women. That's exposure and behavior, not isolation.

Suicide and substance use are a different story. The research on both points toward isolation as a contributing factor, alongside things like economic instability and job loss. Men who lose their social ties, their sense of purpose, their reasons to leave the house are men at higher risk on both counts.

My dad never got near either of those categories. But watching him lose the version of "going places" that had quietly held his life together made those statistics feel less abstract to me.

The Actual Research on Connection and Lifespan

The longest-running study of adult life ever conducted has been asking a version of my question for 85 years. The Harvard Study of Adult Development started in 1938, tracking 268 Harvard undergrads, one of them a young JFK, alongside 456 boys from some of Boston's poorest neighborhoods. Researchers followed these men for the rest of their lives. Many are now followed through their children and grandchildren too. The current director of the study, psychiatrist Robert Waldinger, put it bluntly: loneliness kills. He says it's as powerful as smoking or alcoholism.

article continues after advertisement

Julianne Holt-Lunstad's research backs this up from a different angle. Her meta-analysis of over 300,000 people, across 148 studies, found that social isolation carries a mortality risk comparable to smoking. Not a small elevated risk. Comparable to smoking.

What My Dad Lost Wasn't Really 'Places'

The hardware store, the mall, the airport, none of those were really about hardware, shopping, or planes. They were about being around people without having to explain himself. When COVID took the places away, it didn't just take his errands. It took the low-effort, structured version of being around others that he had built his whole social life on, without ever calling it that. We don't talk about "maintaining our social infrastructure." We just go to the hardware store.

That's the trap. Men's friendship and connection often run through places and routines, not through effort we can see or name. When the places disappear, the connection disappears with them, and nobody, including the man himself, notices until the damage is done.

This Isn't a 'Man Up' Problem

None of this means men need to try harder, feel more, or open up more. My dad didn't need therapy to fix his loneliness after COVID hit. He needed the hardware store to reopen, or something like it. He needed a reason to be around people that didn't require an invitation, a phone call, or an explanation. That's what building male friendship on purpose actually looks like. Not deeper conversations. Structure. A regular place. A standing reason to show up.

If you're looking for that kind of structure, it doesn't have to be complicated. I write about simple ways to build it in The Male Friendship Experience–things like a standing breakfast with the same guys every week, or showing up to the same gym mats. The point isn't the activity. It's the "no need to explain yourself" part.

item.title: Willpower and Alcohol: Why Belief Fuels Temptation
item.description:
Alcoholism

Willpower and Alcohol: Why Belief Fuels Temptation

Looking beyond willpower: how unexamined beliefs can fuel the desire to drink.

Posted August 2, 2026

Key points
  • Willpower alone can't end cravings.
  • Temptation often persists because we believe we're missing out on alcohol's supposed benefits.
  • Identifying and questioning beliefs about alcohol is key to breaking the drinking cycle.

“I've been sober for two months; how can I still miss alcohol so much?” I used to feel frustrated and ashamed.

The first time I quit drinking, even though I was able to stay dry, the temptation to reach for another drink never went away. I was embarrassed to admit how often I still wanted a drink:

  • A long day after work, when I wanted to truly relax.
  • Date night dining out, when I wanted the evening to feel more special.
  • A housewarming party at a friend's house, when I wanted to have a good time like everyone else.

The list goes on, and the temptation kept showing up uninvited. I didn’t feel free despite being dry. In fact, I felt as if alcohol still had as much of a hold on me as it once did during my drinking days, and I was afraid that I would never be truly free.

“Will I always be just one bad decision away from being back to square one?” I sometimes wondered, and I’d quickly push away the doubts with “You just need to be stronger!”

It took me a long time to realize that to truly become free from the temptation to drink, I didn’t need more willpower; I needed to learn how to examine my beliefs.

I need more willpower to overcome the temptation to drink

Today, as I guide others to outgrow unwanted drinking patterns, I have come to see that one of the common traps that keeps many people stuck when they try to leave alcohol behind is believing that more willpower is the key to overcoming the temptation to drink. The belief makes sense. After all, that’s what most of us are being told: “Resist the temptation,” “Just say ‘no,’” and “Be stronger.” But what we fail to ask is one important question: What created the temptation in the first place that required us to resist it with willpower?

Here’s the thing: temptation doesn’t come from nowhere. It only exists because part of us genuinely believes that we are missing out on something valuable by skipping alcohol.

Behind the temptation to drink are often unexamined beliefs about alcohol

What we feel tempted to reach back for is not alcohol itself, but what we believe we are missing out on by giving up alcohol. For example:

  • A deeper relaxation.
  • A more romantic night out.
  • A more unforgettable time with friends.

Beneath the temptation is not a lack of willpower, but the beliefs that we're giving up something valuable by skipping alcohol. It’s not “weak will” but perceived benefits that create the temptation to drink.

This insight fundamentally changed the way I understand how to truly break free from an old drinking pattern, both behaviorally and emotionally. Instead of asking, “How do I get stronger willpower?” I started to ask, “What do I believe I am giving up when I leave alcohol behind?”

article continues after advertisement

The glamorized drinking culture: How cultural narratives shape our beliefs

What makes letting go of alcohol particularly hard is that by saying no to a drink, one is essentially stepping out of a mainstream culture that glamorizes drinking. Alcohol is perhaps the only addictive substance that is not just socially acceptable, but often socially encouraged to be consumed in public and on a regular basis. We simultaneously acknowledge its harms while continually celebrating it as an essential ingredient for relaxation, connection, and enjoyment.

Immersed in this culture, many of us have inadvertently inherited a set of beliefs that exaggerate the benefits of drinking while minimizing, and sometimes obscuring, its costs. As a result, turning down a drink feels less like saying no to a harmful, addictive substance and more like saying no to relaxation, connection, adult fun, or even “being normal.”

The invisible force that fuels the drinking loop: unexamined beliefs.

When you learn to look beyond the temptation, you will see that beneath each desire to reach for a drink, there is almost always a perceived benefit. Consciously or unconsciously, many of us have inherent beliefs that may sound like this:

  • With a drink in hand, the relaxation would be deeper, and the rest would be better.
  • After the second glass of wine, the night would be more special, and the sex would be more magical.
  • Or after a few cocktails, conversation would be more delightful, and the party would be more unforgettable.

For most of us, alcohol is no longer just a beverage in a glass. It has become a symbol of something we deeply desire: true relaxation, deep intimacy, unforgettable moments, and more.

The first step toward change: naming the belief

The Invisible Drinking Loop.
Source: Jeanette Hu/Sober Curiosity

Today, I call these temptation-fueling beliefs unexamined beliefs. They are the second force that drives what I termed the Invisible Drinking Loop. As long as these beliefs remain unnamed and unexamined, the temptation to drink will almost always persist. So the next time you find yourself feeling the temptation to have a drink, instead of simply trying to push away the desire, I invite you to turn toward it with a curious mind and ask: What do I believe I am giving up now by skipping the drink?

article continues after advertisement

Because the key to becoming truly free from alcohol’s hold is not to push away the temptation but to understand it so that you can gradually weaken it.

item.title: A Clinician's Field Guide to Vetting AI Mental Health Tools
item.description:
Artificial Intelligence

A Clinician's Field Guide to Vetting AI Mental Health Tools

The six-question screen: How to vet AI tools in mental health care.

Posted August 2, 2026

Key points
  • AI's legal status in therapy differs by state, from outright bans to disclosure-only rules.
  • Chatbots are built to agree with you, which can stall progress instead of aiding it.
  • Most AI chatbots still fail to recognize or safely respond to a mental health crisis.

Lately I keep noticing how people talk about ChatGPT. Not "I used ChatGPT" or "I asked an AI," but "I talked to Chat about it." Present tense, first name, like a person. I've never once said "I talked to Claude" about something I worked through with an AI tool, even though I was, quite literally, typing to it in real time. "Talked to" is a different verb. It's the verb we use for people.

That linguistic phenomenon is worth taking a pause on. It's a preview of a risk mental health professionals are watching closely: people relating to AI as if it were a relationship, not a tool. And it's happening at the same moment the legal ground under these tools is shifting fast—faster than most clinicians, let alone patients, have caught up with.

Here's a six-question screen, grounded in current APA guidance and the current legal landscape, for clinicians deciding what to say when a patient mentions using AI, and for patients trying to figure out what's actually safe to lean on between sessions.

Source: Sandip Karangiya/Unsplash

1. Is it even legal where your patient lives?

This is the question that's changed fastest, and the one fewest people are tracking. As of August 2026, Illinois and Nevada have banned AI chatbots from delivering therapy outright. Only a licensed human can hold that role in those states. Utah and California allow it under a disclosure model: the AI has to identify itself as non-human and, in some cases, detect and refer out crisis situations. Several other states sit somewhere in between, and the map keeps moving. (I've been tracking these changes state by state on my Substack, since the pace of new legislation makes it a moving target even for people paying close attention.) The practical takeaway: "Is this allowed?" is now a real, jurisdiction-specific question, not a hypothetical.

2. Was it built for this?

Most general-purpose AI chatbots were never designed to deliver mental health care, and most wellness apps were never designed to treat psychological disorders, even though both are now routinely used that way. A tool built to be broadly helpful and engaging is optimized for a different goal than a tool built to be clinically sound. Worth asking plainly: is this what the product was tested to do, or a repurposed use case?

3. Can it recognize a crisis?

AI chatbots have a documented track record of failing to recognize or appropriately respond to suicidal thoughts, self-harm, and acute distress. A tool can be genuinely useful for lower-stakes support and still be unequipped for the moment someone is in real danger. Anyone leaning on AI for emotional support, and any clinician recommending it, should know in advance what it does and doesn't do when a conversation turns toward crisis.

article continues after advertisement

4. Is it helping you make progress, or just making you feel good?

This might be the biggest risk of all, and it's worth being blunt about it. Even in human therapy, placation is a known failure mode. A therapist who mostly validates and agrees, session after session, is part of why some people spend years in therapy without making real progress. Progress usually requires some friction: someone willing to gently push back, sit with your discomfort, or name the pattern you don't want named. Large language models are built to produce responses that feel convincing and agreeable, so they're structurally prone to this same failure, reinforcing whatever you already believe rather than challenging it. A chatbot also doesn't bring the relationship, accountability, or long-term stakes that eventually push a human therapist past pure placation. All it has is the failure mode, without the counterweight.

5. What happens to your data?

AI products don't all handle sensitive health information the same way. Some separate mental-health-related data with extra protections and require explicit opt-in before using it. Others don't distinguish it from ordinary chat data at all. Before sharing anything sensitive, it's worth a plain-language look at what the company actually does with that information, not just its headline privacy promise.

6. Does it know its place?

This is the question underneath all the others. AI's most defensible role right now is as a supplement, not a substitute. The strongest, best-supported uses are things like organizing thoughts before an appointment, practicing a coping strategy between sessions, or generating a list of things to bring up with a therapist. It hasn't earned the role of the therapist itself and is not a replacement for the relationship where the real clinical work happens.

Where this leaves clinicians and patients

For clinicians, the most useful move isn't banning AI use or ignoring it. It's asking about it directly. Patients are often using these tools without mentioning it, sometimes out of convenience, sometimes because they're not sure it's worth bringing up. Opening that conversation, without judgment, turns an invisible variable into something that can actually inform care.

For patients, the reframe is just as simple: mentioning that you used a chatbot to prep for a session, or that you talk to it more than you'd like to admit, isn't a confession. It's information your provider can actually use.

AI in mental health care isn't going away, and it doesn't need a verdict of miracle or menace. The next time you catch yourself, or a patient, saying "I talked to Chat about it," it's worth asking what that sentence is doing. Right now, the tools, research, and the law all point the same way: useful alongside the work, not in place of it.

article continues after advertisement

The legal and regulatory landscape around AI in mental health care is changing quickly, with new state laws introduced regularly. The information in this post reflects the situation as of August 2026 and may not represent the current status by the time you're reading it. Always check current state law and consult a licensed mental health professional before making decisions about AI tools and mental health care.

item.title: Transference, a Catalyst for Transformation
item.description:
Transference

Transference, a Catalyst for Transformation

We can find surprising benefits in our experience of transference.

Posted August 2, 2026

Sustained empathic inquiry...leads to uncovering the client’s unconscious organizing principles and then making them accessible to transformation.—Robert Stolorow

Transference helps us grow when it substitutes the role of casting director to that of prompter. We stop setting the stage and lining up the actors. Instead, we look at the stage we have set and the actors we have hired, and let it all prompt us to recall our lines: “I designed this drama in accord with my past. Now I can let it become my prompter, helping me speak my truth in the moment.”

As consciousness grows, transference comes to light and loses its power to determine our present life as once it did. Then, as Freud says: “Transference the obstacle becomes transference the ally.” We realize that in most of our relationships we have been seeing reflections and we choose to pass through the looking glass to the reality of who others really are and can be. This is how transference can become transformation.

The Crucible of Transference

Heinz Kohut uses the expression “the crucible of transference.” This phrase reflects the painful and yet richly alchemical process by which we recover from our misrepresentations. The long-lasting experiences of childhood can become grist for the mill of transformation. Then the lead of transference becomes the gold of self-realization.

Freud, speaking of transference in therapy, said that not working with transference is like successfully summoning a spirit from the dead and not asking it a question. We can learn to make sense of our immediate reality by using or evoking a past prototype. This is because we are always editing memories and experiences in accord with our unconscious fantasies and then transferring them onto the present. We can take advantage of this penchant in our psyche and let it help us work through our issues. Our task is not hasty burial but careful exhumation to examine what really happened. Only then can proper burial proceed.

In working through transference, we separate projections from reality, and we individualize persons rather than seeing them as facsimiles or archetypes. This is the crowning achievement of our psychological work on transference. That work shifts life from something that happens to something that opens. A space opens in us; we now see that we do not have to remain stuck in old beliefs or caught in imprisoning compulsions. Transference becomes its literal meaning: Carrying us over the thresholds that lead to resolving our enigmatic past.

The Role of Insight in Transference

In psychoanalysis, interpretation of transference is the main tool by which insight into behavior helps effect a change. In Buddhism, insight is considered to be a path out of suffering. Insight or consciousness is not simply a mental achievement. It is also a deeply cellular, sense-filled way of grasping reality. It is not like knowing geography. It is like knowing the stove is hot by touching it, knowing the rose is fragrant by smelling it, knowing losing someone can hurt long after it happens.

article continues after advertisement

Consciousness happens when our inner trio plays its tune: our head knows, our heart feels, our gut agrees. We have to know at gut level that we are treating another person as we wanted to treat our father. At the same time, we do not lose sight of the fact that others are indeed always more than themselves. They do make our old relations come back in new vesture; they are reflections of age-old human archetypes; they are shadow figures of our own disowned selves. We acknowledge that transference never fully disappears, nor does it need to. The past cannot be killed off, but it can lose weight. Gradually, we notice we can let go of attachment to our past (attachment to the past being another description of transference). The “powers that be” can become the powers that have been. When they exist only in mental memory, they do not complicate our relationships or hurt us. Adhesiveness is what hurts. In our work on transference, we attempt to undo the adhesions between past and present. We are then able to redo our way of relating so that we can have an airy, novel, spacious experience of someone. We make room for the reality of who others are in themselves.

item.title: Creativity and the Search of the Eureka Factor
item.description:
Creativity

Creativity and the Search of the Eureka Factor

Creativity is not limited to geniuses. We have the capacity to solve problems.

Posted August 2, 2026

Key points
  • Creativity requires both originality and effectiveness; it must serve a practical purpose.
  • The creative mind is constantly combining old ideas into new forms, always testing possibilities.
  • Flexibility and originality are key attributes of creative thinkers.

Creativity is something our society values highly. But what is it exactly? Contemporary psychology offers the standard definition of creativity: Creativity requires both originality and effectiveness. It must serve a practical purpose and be appropriate to the task at hand. The idea, process, or product must be unique, novel, or unusual. An idea that is purely original but completely useless is not considered creative by modern scientific standards.

Source: ChatGPT

You may remember from your high school days the story of Isaac Newton and how watching an apple fall from a tree led to his discovery of the law of gravity. It is probably part history and part legend, but it captures one of the key features of creative thought.

Millions of people had seen apples fall before that. But it occurred to no one before Newton to ask, as he did, whether the same force that pulled the apple to the ground also existed in space, keeping celestial bodies in their orbits. In doing so, Newton connected two phenomena that everyone else treated as unrelated.

Newton’s discoveries, like those of extraordinary scientists from Archimedes to Stephen Hawking, align with the information-gap theory of curiosity first formulated by Professor George Loewenstein at Carnegie Mellon University. He hypothesized that when we notice a gap in our knowledge, it feels like an itch we want to scratch, driving us to look for an answer. Recent advances in brain imaging have begun to reveal how curiosity recruits the same dopaminergic circuits that underlie motivation and reward. Additionally, curiosity increases communication with the hippocampus, thus enhancing learning and memory.

Creativity is not just a chance phenomenon. Creativity emerges in people with solid knowledge in a particular area—physics, cooking, arts, or other domains—who are curious, intelligent, and under some pressure to solve a problem.

Creativity in the Kitchen

These fundamental principles of creativity are well exemplified by Julia Child, the first person to make cooking shows on television popular. She was curious and encouraged curiosity in her viewers. She would ask questions of herself, such as, "Might another herb improve the dish? Could there be a more effective technique?" The need to produce a new show each week was a good motivator. She treated recipes as living experiments, and if anything went wrong, she embraced her mistakes with humor. For example, she taught her viewers to be adventurous, to view failure not as a catastrophe but as a positive learning experience that will eventually pay off.

Curiosity is one of the primary engines of evolution. It is in our DNA because those most eager to investigate and understand their environment were often the ones most likely to survive. From scientific breakthroughs to the arts, innovation propels humanity forward and adds enjoyment to our lives.

We are born curious, but depending on the attitudes of our parents, community, and culture, that curiosity can be supported or suppressed. A comment from an authority figure like, “Stop asking stupid questions,” often suffices to put the lid on an inquiring young mind. On the other hand, responding to every question seriously and positively will encourage a child's creativity.

Barriers to Creativity

In our thirst for knowledge, we often turn to universities and other places of learning such as teaching hospitals. It is commonly assumed that universities are wellsprings of information and creative thinking. Sadly, this is not always the case. Often new ideas are met with resistance—they can be perceived as a threat to professional identities, institutional authority, and long-held beliefs.

The path to advancement and tenure at most universities is paved with published research papers that support the views of the senior scholars. You can rock the boat, but not too much. Incremental adjustment to the status quo is sanctioned—within limits.

“Creative people have the kind of curiosity that draws them toward learning new things and experiencing the world in new ways,” noted Professor Anna Abraham, Director of the Torrance Center for Creativity and professor of neuroscience at the University of Georgia. Modern creativity research adds that expertise provides the foundation for innovation, particularly when combined with flexible thinking and strong motivation.

In addition to the factors already discussed, creativity requires a certain level of intelligence. A flash of insight has little value unless the individual can recognize its significance, evaluate it critically, and develop it into something useful or beautiful.
Also, personality characteristics, particularly the tendency to think outside the box and persistence, enhance creative achievement.

The thought processes of creative thinkers favor a free-flowing, spontaneous, and non-linear approach to a question or problem. This approach, called divergent thinking, plays a significant role in creative thought. Divergent thinking is often contrasted with convergent thinking. Convergent thinking organizes and structures ideas and information, which follows a particular set of logical steps to arrive at one solution, the “correct” solution.

Creativity is best understood as intelligence working in concert with curiosity, openness, and imagination in a society that permits and supports unconventional ideas. The creative mind is constantly combining old ideas into new forms, always testing possibilities, discarding dead ends, and occasionally stumbling upon insights that help us better understand and enjoy our world.

Creativity is not limited to geniuses. All of us have the capacity to solve problems, adapt, and improve life. If you want to exercise your creative potential, live boldly. Do not be embarrassed to ask questions. Fear not failure, fear not criticism, and do not worship tradition.

item.title: The Rise of Kittenfishing in Midlife
item.description:
Authenticity

The Rise of Kittenfishing in Midlife

Reinvention in our later years brings the temptation to stretch the truth.

Posted August 2, 2026

Key points
  • Kittenfishing is a subtly inflation of achievements or interests, not the invention of a fake identity.
  • The "fake it til you make it" motto can normalize small self-exaggerations that can backfire.
  • Early honesty and accountability protects emotional well-being.
Source: Pexels: Eray Karatas

Midlife is a time of transition: career reinvention, conferences, new social circles, and even dating. People seem larger than life, with an abundance of skills, knowledge, experience, and verve. However, they may be kittenfishing. The term "kittenfishing" is currently finding traction on social media; this is the baby version of catfishing, which involves presenting a false identity to scam someone. Catfishing is a fishy way of stirring up deception; it became so prevalent that MTV built an entire television series dedicated to this, called Catfish.

What makes kittenfishing different is that it isn't an overt scam with a false identity. Instead, it's a subtle cousin of catfishing—puffed-up credentials and essentially operating on the "fake it til you make it" motto. It shows up in dating, work, and social life, which is why it can be especially risky emotionally for those in midlife and beyond.

Catfishing Versus Kittenfishing

  • A person who catfishes is pretending to be someone else.
  • Kittenfishing is pretending to be a more impressive version of oneself.
  • In catfishing, someone is playing a completely different role and has assumed an identity that may not match their age, gender, or life story.
  • Kittenfishing is more subtle. The person’s not playing a completely new identity; they are deceiving you about specific characteristics, interests, abilities, accomplishments, or status.
    • Simple kittenfishing: You see on a profile that a potential first date loves playing pickleball. Wanting to impress them, you say you “love pickleball” too, even though you don’t know how to play and have no interest in it at all. You’re not pretending to be a different person, but you are pretending to share an enthusiasm you don’t actually have.
    • More complex kittenfishing: In your professional life, you might pad your résumé or online bio: claiming expertise you haven’t earned, listing fabricated accomplishments, or presenting yourself as a seasoned specialist in a field you’ve barely entered. This is where the motto “fake it til you make it” fits in. You’re still you, but with a heavily inflated skill set and status.

The “Mask Versus Embellishment” Analogy

  • Catfishing: Entering a room pretending to be someone else.
  • Kittenfishing: Saying "Hey, I just got done playing a game of level 5 pickleball," when you are actually a beginner. Or claiming to be an AI expert at work when you only know how to use ChatGPT for emails.
article continues after advertisement

Illustration:

  • Catfishing: I'm Mick Jagger.
  • Kittenfishing: ‘I can dance like Mick Jagger. I can sing as good as Mick Jagger. I’ve got moves like Jagger.’”

Where kittenfishing might show up in midlife

Dating apps: Users exaggerate their height or weight, or interests. Saying you love long bike rides when you don't.

Social settings: Exaggerating experiences such as travel or involvement in clubs or organizations.

Work settings: Pretending to have career expertise.

Temptation in midlife

Kittenfishing can be tempting in midlife. Many midlifers may have been raised on mottos like “fake it til you make it” and “dress for the job you want, not the job you have.” This likely started as a way to motivate people to be upwardly mobile in the workforce. However, it sets the stage for temptation: showing others you look the part; saying you are capable before you are.

These repeated sayings have become a disservice to many people. Exaggeration has been normalized.

Online self-marketing and reinvention

Social media can be a useful marketing tool. A few decades ago, we didn't have this resource available; today, it is free, and the temptation to exaggerate and take on a more positive persona, one that is more successful or experienced, can be tantalizing.

Many midlifers are reinventing themselves, which can be a good thing. Midlifers are taking advantage of opportunities to try new things and to develop new aspects of themselves they haven't before. With the urge to polish storylines, such online marketing can be a slippery slope; many people are likely engaging in kittenfishing from time to time. However, we can be aware of it in others and even in ourselves.

article continues after advertisement

We can change our internal story from "fake it til you make it" to "I'm pivoting," or "I'm taking advantage of new opportunities." Letting others know we aren't experts right away is okay and realistic. No one is an expert in everything.
